title: The Sea Between Us
author: Mara Voss
description: Marine cartographer Lena Orlov returns to the storm-battered island where she grew up after her father disappears during an unauthorized survey voyage. The only person willing to help is her estranged older sister, Anya, who stayed behind to run the family boatyard and has spent twelve years resenting Lena's departure. Their search follows a chain of hand-drawn tide maps into a protected channel threatened by a luxury marina project. As the sisters reconstruct their father's final days, they uncover a quiet campaign to erase the island's fishing history and must decide whether saving their community is worth exposing a painful family secret. Rich with salt-air atmosphere and closely observed sibling tension, the novel balances a slow-burning mystery with an intimate story about grief, belonging, and the imperfect routes people take back to one another. Recommended for readers who enjoy character-driven coastal fiction and emotionally grounded environmental themes.

title: Midnight at the Paper Moon
author: Theo Vale
description: In 1932 Chicago, failed vaudeville illusionist Silas Grey accepts a night job at the Paper Moon, a photography studio that manufactures glamorous portraits for people who cannot afford glamorous lives. When a customer vanishes after leaving a glass negative covered in tiny coded scratches, Silas and the studio's sharp-eyed retoucher, Ruth Bell, are pulled into a mystery involving a shuttered theater, counterfeit relief vouchers, and a magician everyone believes died in a fire. Each clue depends on an old stage trick, but the final deception is rooted in the city's very real desperation. The story moves with the snap of a backstage caper while giving its eccentric ensemble room to become a makeshift family. Atmospheric without being grim, it is a good fit for readers who like clever puzzles, Depression-era settings, dry humor, and mysteries solved through observation rather than violence.

title: The Orchard Book
author: Nina Callow
description: Horticulturist Nina Callow offers a practical, visually guided handbook for growing fruit in spaces ranging from balcony containers to small suburban yards. Instead of organizing the book only by species, she begins with the decisions that determine success: local chill hours, pollination partners, rootstock size, soil drainage, sun patterns, and realistic maintenance time. Detailed profiles cover apples, pears, stone fruit, figs, citrus, persimmons, and lesser-known choices for hot or cold climates. Month-by-month checklists explain pruning, feeding, thinning, netting, harvesting, and early signs of common pests, while illustrated troubleshooting pages help readers distinguish cosmetic damage from urgent disease. Callow is candid about how long trees take to bear and includes compact plans for one-tree, three-tree, and patio orchards. The tone is encouraging but precise, making this a useful reference for first-time growers and experienced gardeners planning a more resilient, water-conscious home orchard.

title: Atlas of Small Wonders
author: June Bell
description: This illustrated science atlas invites young readers to investigate the tiny systems hiding in ordinary places. Twelve oversized maps zoom in on a teaspoon of pond water, the underside of a city leaf, a pinch of garden soil, a tide pool, a beehive wall, a kitchen sourdough starter, and other miniature worlds. Each spread combines labeled artwork with short explanations of how organisms move, eat, cooperate, compete, and change their surroundings. Sidebars suggest safe, low-cost observations using a magnifying glass, notebook, flashlight, or clear jar, and recurring scale markers help children understand just how small each subject really is. Author June Bell avoids talking down to readers and clearly separates what can be seen at home from what requires a microscope. Designed for independent browsing or family reading, the book rewards curiosity and shows that meaningful scientific discovery can begin in a sidewalk crack or a drop of water.

title: A Glass Horizon
author: Amari West
description: Decades after rising seas forced millions into mobile desert cities, engineer Sanaa Rook maintains the glass skins that pull drinking water from the night air. During a routine repair she discovers a sealed observation chamber containing recordings of coastlines that official archives insist never existed. The images are tied to the city's navigation system and to Sanaa's missing childhood memories, making their authenticity dangerous to both the ruling transit corporation and the families who depend on the city staying in motion. With a union medic, a teenage map thief, and an obsolete maintenance intelligence, Sanaa traces the recordings to a stationary settlement hidden beyond the approved routes. The novel pairs large-scale climate speculation with the tactile details of keeping a fragile machine alive. Its central mystery asks who gets to preserve a place, who profits when history is made portable, and whether a community built for survival can choose to stop running.

title: Salt Letters
author: Mara Voss
description: For twenty years, translator Iris Dane has exchanged one letter every month with Tomoe Arakida, a ceramic artist living on a remote island across the Pacific. They have never met and have agreed never to speak by phone. When Tomoe's letters abruptly begin arriving out of order, each postmarked years earlier, Iris travels to the island carrying the complete correspondence. She finds a community preparing to relocate before the only ferry service ends and learns that Tomoe has used their letters as the glaze notes for hundreds of bowls distributed among departing residents. To understand the sequence, Iris must read her own life as carefully as she once read Tomoe's words. Quiet, spare, and deeply attentive to objects, the novel explores how friendship can be both intimate and incomplete, how translation changes the translator, and how ordinary records become an archive when a place is about to disappear.

title: The Night Cartographer
author: Theo Vale
description: Seventeen-year-old Ren Calder maps streets that exist only between sunset and dawn. These temporary lanes carry bakers to tomorrow morning, ghosts to forgotten houses, and couriers around impossible distances, but every route disappears from paper at first light. When an entire neighborhood fails to return with the sunrise, Ren is blamed for drawing an illegal shortcut through the city's oldest map. Clearing his name means partnering with Mina, an apprentice lamplighter whose family vanished with the district, and following a trail of erased landmarks into the archive beneath city hall. There they discover that the official daytime map has been quietly consuming the night streets for generations. Inventive geography drives the adventure, while the friendship at its center grows through mistakes, divided loyalties, and hard-won trust. The book suits readers who enjoy accessible fantasy systems, puzzle-like cities, brisk danger, and heroes who solve problems by noticing what powerful people have chosen not to record.

title: Small Weather
author: June Bell
description: Naturalist June Bell spends one year tracking weather at human scale: the cold pocket beside a laundromat wall, the afternoon wind between two apartment towers, the first block where rain becomes snow, and the rooftop garden that blooms weeks before the park below. Across twenty-four short essays, she combines field notes, interviews with gardeners and maintenance workers, and clear explanations of shade, thermal mass, drainage, air pressure, and urban heat. The collection is less a guide to forecasting than an invitation to notice how buildings, trees, pavement, and habits create many local seasons inside a single ZIP code. Simple observation prompts at the end of each essay help readers keep their own neighborhood log without specialized equipment. Reflective but grounded in science, the book will appeal to walkers, gardeners, amateur naturalists, and anyone curious about why the weather reported at the airport rarely matches the weather outside their door.
